riddle:
Five weeks out of Reykjavík, north of Vestmannaeyjar, our trawler's hold reeks of ammonia and clanks with steel plates.
At dawn the pick of the trip was split: gutted whole cod went straight into those plates, but fillets cut from the very same fish were banned from them.
Grimsby cabled double money for "the freshest"; the man in yellow oilskins cabled back, "You'll have Tuesday's, never today's."
Today's fillets lay in slush ice a full twenty-four hours before freezing, while older, duller flesh went in first — why?
chars: Hrefna, a Grimsby fish importer; Óli, the trawler's refrigeration engineer
story: Óli runs the ammonia plate-freezer plant on a factory trawler that lands nothing fresh, only frozen blocks five weeks later, so what Hrefna is really buying is how a block behaves in her thawing room, not hours out of the sea. Gutted cod can be frozen stiff pre-rigor because the backbone restrains the flesh, but a fillet freed from the spine and frozen before rigor has passed goes into thaw rigor on defrosting — contracting by up to a third of its length, turning tough and weeping red drip — so today's fillets must sit in 0 °C slush ice for the roughly twenty-four hours cod needs to come out of rigor, while yesterday's, already through it, freeze first.
fact:
REAL

Thaw rigor is a documented phenomenon: fish fillets frozen before rigor mortis has passed contract strongly on thawing (reported up to about 30–50%), becoming tough and losing drip, so processors hold fillets until they are past rigor (or freeze whole gutted fish, where the backbone restrains the flesh).

Whole gutted fish can go straight into the ammonia plate freezers because the backbone holds the muscle in place. So he lets today's fillets pass through rigor in slush ice for a day first, and he cables Grimsby that the only top-quality fillets he can deliver are Tuesday's, not today's.

Forty-six winters it has grown lighter, and nobody has ever topped it up, though it is barely a third full.
Her hydrometer reads 40.4, so she has booked the bottling hall for Tuesday — four days before that cask's forty-seventh birthday.

Ryōgoku, Tokyo, May 2012: on day four the old man dragged his 3–1 man off the clay over one swollen knee — his second ruined month running.
The doctor's letter bought nothing, and the June sheet dropped him a single rung.
"A gift," the old man said. "Ten wins by day fifteen of July — or thirty-three across the next three."

chars: Ryūhō (the 3–1 man); Tetsuzan-oyakata (sumo stablemaster)
story: Ryūhō was an ōzeki already kadoban after 7–8 in March, so when Tetsuzan-oyakata deliberately pulled him out at 3–1 on day four of May, every remaining bout was scored a loss — sumo grants no injury exemption, making the doctor's letter waste paper — and the June banzuke demoted him to sekiwake.
